data.text/markdown:
Pose graphs and loop closures

This notebook uses the MRPT Python wheel (pip install mrpt3) to build the pose graph of a robot that drives through a small city-block route and revisits some places, and then optimizes it. It uses three MRPT modules:
  • mrpt.poses: SE(2) poses (CPose2D), their composition a + b and relative pose a - b.
  • mrpt.graphs: the pose graph (CNetworkOfPoses2D), its spanning-tree estimate and shortest paths.
  • mrpt.graphslam: nonlinear least-squares optimization of the graph (optimize_graph_spa_levmarq).
In graph SLAM, each robot pose is a node and each relative measurement is an edge: odometry links consecutive poses, and a loop closure links two poses at the same place, visited at different times. Odometry alone drifts without bound; loop closures are what tie the trajectory back together. Move the sliders: everything below is recomputed.

data.text/html: Parameters

data.text/markdown:
1. Ground truth and simulated measurements

The robot drives along the streets of a 3 × 2 block grid (10 m blocks), recording a pose every meter. Odometry measures the relative pose between consecutive poses, gt[i + 1] - gt[i], corrupted by noise. A loop closure is the relative pose between two poses close in space but far apart in time, here with a small error (5 cm, 1°), as if obtained by matching two laser scans.

2. The pose graph and its initial estimate

CNetworkOfPoses2D.insertEdge(i, j, z) adds the measurement z: the pose of node j as seen from node i. With odometry only, the global pose of each node is the composition of all the edges before it (dead reckoning), and its error grows with the distance traveled. dijkstra_nodes_estimate() computes the global pose of every node by composing edges along the shortest path (fewest edges) from the root node 0. Loop closures act as shortcuts: many nodes become fewer edges away from the root, so their estimate accumulates less drift. This spanning-tree estimate is the usual starting point of graph SLAM optimizers.

The graph has 211 nodes and 216 edges (6 loop closures). The farthest node is 50 edges away from the root (it would be 210 with odometry alone).
Estimate Position RMSE vs. ground truth (m)
Dead reckoning (odometry only) 6.68
Spanning tree (dijkstra_nodes_estimate) 2.05
Edges that the spanning-tree estimate does not satisfy (red in the plot): 6.

data.text/markdown: dijkstra_path(0, 210) returns the shortest path from the root (black square) to the selected node (star): 12 edges, instead of 210 along the odometry chain. Composing these edges gives the pose that dijkstra_nodes_estimate() assigned to that node, [-0.210065 10.232076 -175.317859deg], while its ground truth is [0.000000 10.000000 -180.000000deg].

3. Where does the error go?

The spanning tree satisfies exactly the edges it is made of. Every other edge (red above) carries all the inconsistency accumulated along the two branches of the tree that meet there, and the estimate jumps at those places. The position error grows with the number of edges to the root, not with the time at which a pose was recorded:

4. Optimization: spreading the error over the loops

The final step of graph SLAM is a nonlinear least-squares optimization that moves all nodes at once to satisfy every edge as well as possible. Each edge residual is weighted by the information matrix (inverse covariance) of its measurement, so precise loop closures pull harder than noisy odometry. In MRPT, edges with uncertainty are CPosePDFGaussianInf objects in a CNetworkOfPoses2DInf graph, and optimize_graph_spa_levmarq() runs Sparse Pose Adjustment with Levenberg-Marquardt, starting from the spanning-tree estimate.

Levenberg-Marquardt stopped after 8 iterations, with a total squared (Mahalanobis) error of 26.1.
Estimate Position RMSE vs. ground truth (m)
Dead reckoning (odometry only) 6.68
Spanning tree (dijkstra_nodes_estimate) 2.05
Optimized (optimize_graph_spa_levmarq) 0.25

The optimizer has no single "seam" left: the inconsistency of each loop is shared by all its edges, in proportion to their uncertainty, so the error no longer jumps where two branches of the spanning tree meet.

5. Saving the graph

Pose graphs can be saved in the standard g2o text format, readable by MRPT's graphslam-engine application and other graph optimizers. Edges with uncertainty include the upper triangle of their information matrix:

Run it on your computer (Linux, Python 3.11 to 3.14): 
uvx marimo edit --sandbox https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MRPT/mrpt-notebooks/main/notebooks/pose_graph_slam.py
More MRPT Python examples: mrpt_examples_py.
